paper.title: Characterization of clinical Ralstonia strains and their taxonomic position

open_questions.q: Do the 18 clinical Ralstonia strains have linkable clinical metadata (source body site, infection type, patient outcome, comorbidities, prior antibiotic exposure) that would let ANIb group membership (D1, D2, E1, E2, F, G) be tested for association with clinical phenotype rather than only genomic distance?
open_questions.basis: The paper is a taxonomic + AMR-gene study; it groups the 18 strains genomically (ANIb, cgMLST, OXA phylogenies) but the replication artefacts and REPORT.md contain no per-strain clinical metadata (isolation site, patient outcome, etc.). Without this linkage, the taxonomic novelty of Group F (535637) and Group G (551633) cannot be interpreted for clinical importance --- e.g. whether a putative novel species is over-represented in a particular infection type.
next_steps: Query BV-BRC / PATRIC for isolation-source and host metadata attached to each of the 18 BioSample accessions.
Query the paper's supplementary materials and, if incomplete, contact the corresponding author for a de-identified clinical metadata table.
Test group membership vs isolation site / infection outcome using Fisher exact or logistic regression once n per group is known (many groups are singletons, so plan a joined-cohort analysis).

open_questions.q: Is the AMR-gene panel (OXA-22 family + OXA-60 family universal; extra acquired genes only in 545260/545261) complete when re-scored against an expanded isolate set (all BV-BRC Ralstonia genomes, not just 18), and does the 'extra AMR only in 2 strains' finding survive that expansion?
open_questions.basis: The paper's ResFinder analysis (verified in Claim 4) is confined to the 18 sequenced strains. The replication verifies the pattern within that cohort but cannot say whether the 2/18 rate of additional acquired genes generalizes. If most BV-BRC Ralstonia isolates carry additional acquired genes, the paper's clinical implication (that pickettii is intrinsically carbapenemase-carrying but rarely acquires additional resistances) is fragile.
next_steps: Pull all BV-BRC Ralstonia assemblies (>~150 as of 2024) and rerun ResFinder + AMRFinderPlus with a fixed threshold.
Score OXA-22/OXA-60 family carriage across the expanded set and compare hit-rate to the paper's 18/18.
Tabulate additional acquired AMR genes per isolate; compute a 95% CI on the 'extra acquired' rate and compare with the paper's 2/18 = 11.1%.

open_questions.q: How sensitive is the paper's 16S / OXA-22 / OXA-60 phylogenetic group structure (Fig. 3, Fig. 4A, Fig. 4B) to the choice of reference genome (R. pickettii ATCC 27511 NR_043152.1 vs alternate 16S references; AAD12233.1 vs alternate OXA-22 references)?
open_questions.basis: Pass-2 confirmed alignment length matches (OXA-60 271=271; OXA-22 278 vs 279; 16S 1491 uncut) and confirmed D1/D2/E2 monophyly on 18-tip sub-trees, but every phylogeny used a single reference sequence. The published trees use 60 additional 16S references and 11/9 additional OXA references (Supplementary Table 2). It is unknown how much the group-level topology (especially D2 nesting D1/F/G in OXA-60) is a reference-choice artefact vs a genuine long-branch signal.
next_steps: Harvest all reference 16S and OXA-22/OXA-60 accessions from Supplementary Table 2 into data/refs/.
Rebuild the 78-tip 16S, 29-tip OXA-22, 27-tip OXA-60 trees with FastTree GTR/JTT.
Run a reference-swap sensitivity test: rerun each tree with 3-5 alternate type-strain references and quantify RF distance between resulting topologies.

open_questions.q: Are virulence-factor annotations (T3SS, T6SS, siderophores, adhesins, biofilm loci) systematically different between R. pickettii and R. mannitolilytica in the 18-strain cohort, and does that difference (if any) map onto the paper's ANIb groups D vs E?
open_questions.basis: The paper's replication scope is taxonomy + carbapenemase carriage; it does not run VFDB or any virulence-factor annotation. R. pickettii and R. mannitolilytica are both human opportunists but occupy somewhat different clinical niches (R. mannitolilytica is more often reported in bacteremia in immunocompromised hosts), and comparative VF calls could either support or challenge the paper's taxonomic split.
next_steps: Run VFDB (or the BV-BRC virulence factor pipeline) across all 18 assemblies.
Cross-tabulate VF hit counts by ANIb group (D1, D2, E1, E2, F, G) and by species assignment.

Test whether R. mannitolilytica (Group E cluster) carries a distinct VF profile from R. pickettii (Group D cluster); if yes, this would strengthen the paper's argument for keeping them as separate species.

open_questions.q: Does the accessory genome of the 18 strains carry host-pathogen adaptation signals (e.g. horizontally acquired metal-resistance loci, biofilm/quorum-sensing modules, mobile genetic elements) that distinguish clinical Ralstonia from environmental Ralstonia (soil, water, plant-associated), and if so, is that signature stronger in the two putative novel groups F (535637) and G (551633)?
open_questions.basis: The paper (and this replication) focuses on core-genome taxonomy and a narrow AMR panel. Ralstonia is famously environmental (R. solanacearum is a soil-borne plant pathogen), so the interesting biological question --- what does the accessory genome of a clinical isolate carry that an environmental isolate does not, and do the novel groups F/G look more clinical-like or more environmental-like --- is untouched by the paper's scope.
next_steps: Run PIRATE or Roary on the 18 clinical strains plus a comparable-size set of environmental Ralstonia assemblies from BV-BRC to define core vs accessory.
Score accessory-gene functional categories via EggNOG-mapper; compare frequencies clinical vs environmental.

Focus on strains 535637 (Group F) and 551633 (Group G) individually: are their accessory-genome profiles closer to clinical R. pickettii or to environmental Ralstonia, which is a testable prediction about the origin of the putative novel species.

notes: All 5 questions are grounded in what REPORT.md itself flagged as untested or out-of-scope: clinical metadata linkage, cohort expansion of the AMR panel, sensitivity of phylogeny to reference choice, virulence-factor annotation, and clinical-vs-environmental accessory-genome signals.

None of these questions can be answered from the current replication artefacts alone; each requires either additional data pulls (BV-BRC), additional reference accessions (Supplementary Table 2 harvest), or an additional annotation pipeline (VFDB, PIRATE/Roary, EggNOG).

OQ2 and OQ3 are the lowest-cost extensions (bounded compute, no wet lab, no commercial tools); OQ1 depends on metadata availability that may not exist publicly; OQ4 and OQ5 are the largest scope-expansions.
